newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey dusts off aluminium smelter upgrade plan.
newsitem.headline: Turkey dusts off aluminium smelter upgrade plan.

text.p: Turkey's state mining company, Etibank, is reviving a plan shelved five years ago to increase capacity at the country's only primary aluminium smelter for an estimated price tag of $315 million, officials said.

Etibank officials said they were seeking local or foreign investors to set up a venture to execute the plan, whose centrepiece is to upgrade annual capacity at the Seydisehir plant to 100,000 tonnes of primary aluminium from 60,000 tonnes.
"The plan will improve the working atmosphere, enhance the operation performance and ensure an increase in liquid aluminium production," said Ismet Sivrioglu, deputy general manager of Etibank.
A feasibility study and revisions determined the project's investment at $315 million, he told Reuters in a statement. Officials had earlier said the cost might be up to $350 million.
The project, first proposed in 1992 but postponed by the government due to financial difficulties, is envisaged to be completed in four years with a five-year repayment term of funds.
On Wednesday, Etibank invited companies to take part in the joint venture through an announcement in the Official Gazette.
The project envisages uprading the alumina refinery, smelter, and casting and rolling units at the plant, built in early 1960s at Seydisehir, 350 km to the south of Ankara.
According to the project, the plant, which has 248 melting pots, will use a pre-baked anode system instead of the current, unwieldy Soderberg anode method.
"The pre-baked system will improve environmental conditions in accordance with European Union standards," Sivrioglu said.
He said the upgrade would reduce power costs which at 4.65 cents per kilowatt-hour are more than double European smelter costs, despite a 40 percent government subsidy.
The smelter's power is supplied from the nearby state-run Oymapinar hydroelectric plant. Etibank has proposed that it take over the plant to cut power costs.
The project will also reduce unit raw material consumption cost and increase labour productivity, he said but did not elaborate on how this will be acheived.
The project also envisages that the bauxite mine near the plant that produces about 310,000 tonnes annually be leased to the joint venture, which will also be responsible for marketing of products.
The joint venture partners will set up a joint-stock corporation which will finance the fixed capital investment required by the project.

Etibank, which fully owns the smelter, will have a share of 15 to 49 percent in the joint venture, "depending on bids to be made and negotiations to be held," and the total shares of private Turkish and/or foreign investors will not be more than 85 percent, said Sivrioglu.
Etibank's assets to be contributed to the joint venture will be assessed by the partners, he said.
"If the value assessed...appears to be below or above Etibank's share in the joint venture, offset payments...shall be effected," in a schedule.
Etibank's invitation information will be sent to interested companies by May 26 and investors should bid by August 26. --Ankara newsroom, 90-312-446 2940
